doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Central New York's musical talent
summary: Utica-area musicians such as Vince Falcone, the Zito brothers and Sal Nistico, and joking about vowels in names.

bands.name: Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Sometimes you hear people talking about how Utica/Central New York, spawned many great musicians. Do you have a feeling that this area used to be a nice climate for musicians?

Absolutely. And I can’t tell you why, but it goes back to the 30’s and 40’s I guess. And from my era, Vince Falcone, the pianist from Syracuse that became Frank Sinatra’s © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -19-

conductor, and Tony Bennett’s conductor; there was a guy named Torrie Zito of the Zito brothers, Torrie, Art and Ronnie. Ronnie is a drummer and when he was either 18 or 19 he was playing a gig with my former employer Jimmy Cavallo at the Beeches in Rome. Another story, this guy was in the main room with Bobby Darin, and it was the same situation, they heard this drummer and he became Bobby Darin’s drummer. Took him right out of Jimmy’s band. Artie Zito was a bass player. I don’t think he did much outside of Utica but he was well respected; and Torrie Zito was a famous arranger, also a Utica guy. Boy it goes on and on. Everybody, Sal Nistico from Syracuse, the Mangione brothers out of Rochester but still part of the Central New York situation, Chic Esposito, Sal Amico, the Albericos.
And they mostly end with vowels.
That’s part of the magic I think.
You guys used to tell me I needed to change my last name when we played at The Beeches because I was the only — well you know literally I do have a vowel.
